data.title: Why I'm still bearish on LLMs after Navier-Stokes
data.author: jaykru
data.article_summary: 文章认为，当前LLM距离全面替代知识工作者仍很遥远。模型通常只在训练任务的狭窄邻域内有效，稍有变化就可能失败或“奖励投机”。可靠部署需要严谨规格或人工审核，但前者昂贵且难以制定，后者受限于人力和注意力，无法规模化。即使Navier–Stokes等数学证明也只是最理想案例。因此，LLM更像能力很强但需严密监督的实习生，完全自主应用仅适用于少数领域。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：当前大模型的自动化能力、商业估值与未来发展边界。

不同观点：
• 谨慎/看空自动化：棋类实验显示，模型即使知道合法走法仍频繁提出非法操作，且无法击败约1100分的棋手；模型在长时程任务、记忆、时间估计和需求变化处理上也较弱，需要大量监督与护栏。  
• 人机协作派：现阶段更适合“LLM+领域专家”，由人充当监督者和时间锚点；在输出确定、范围狭窄的任务中，模型表现更可靠。有人将其比作“能力很强但不稳定的初级工程师”，可管理大量实习生。  
• 看多/长期乐观：模型能力提升会不断重新定义“简单任务”；前沿实验室虽未必直接取代知识工作者，但能推动架构和技术扩散，未来仍可能出现真正突破。  
• 对估值的争论：一方认为行业约6—7万亿美元估值大致反映当前可自动化的知识工作量；另一方质疑这一推算，认为若能替代价值达50—70万亿美元的知识工作，合理估值应远高于此。  
• 对任务性质的质疑：有人反驳客服是“受控、重复”工作，指出客户求助往往正因为原有流程失控；也有人认为Transformer只是通向递归自我改进等未来技术的工具。

补充讨论：评论还争论能否用芯片行业高验证/设计人员比例类比LLM；批评“按token收费”会诱发冗长、诱导互动和黑暗模式。焦点在于：模型的局部能力是否足以支撑可靠的通用自动化。

49715927.article_content:
why i'm still bearish on LLMs after navier-stokes
[
thank you to claude fable 5.1, holden saberhagen, gabriel kammer, andres erbsen, alice mckean, and tristan wylde-larue for comments on this post
]
i'll begin with a few theses for the reader to chew on:
the frontier labs are priced according to the narrative that they have   produced or will in the very near future produce a fully automated drop-in   replacement for most knowledge workers, but current frontier models need   laborious oversight and guardrails on even the simplest tasks. one misled by   the headline shows of force (navier-stokes, freebsd RCEs, the huggingface   incident) and frontier lab rhetoric into believing meaningful autonomy has   been achieved need only look at the software firms continuing to employ and   hire bottom quartile software engineers who would score far below the models   they supervise on the benchmarks du jour.
the models generalize well only on tasks within a small neighborhood of the   specific tasks they've been trained on, and even then with severe caveats.   the frontier labs have developed a general recipe to teach models almost any
specific
task enjoying clearly defined levels of task performance; many   tasks are covered in the training data; but even small perturbations within a   covered class of task result in outright failure or reward hacking.
the present problem of reward hacking can be solved only by rigorous   specification by domain experts. the time of domain experts is expensive.   rigorous specification is itself a skill, demanding its own expertise outside   of a given problem domain. even many skilled software engineers are bad at   it. for the vast majority of domains, the intersection of domain experts and   specification experts is ludicrously small.
the labor costs of rigorous specification can greatly exceed that of direct   implementation of an informal specification. the hardware engineering world   presents a great case study on this, where a typical CPU project anecdotally   has about three times as many specification and validation engineers as   design engineers and a 5:1 ratio is not
unheard of
.   even worse, many tasks don't admit a convenient spec-and-forget regime where   you write a specification once and continuously implement against it:   rigorous formal specifications frequently evolve in conversation with   insights derived from discoveries made while implementing according to the   informal specification. for tasks that enjoy high level one-and-done   specifications (say an executable ISA specification for a family of CPU   architectures) the costs of verification against such high level   specifications are insurmountable with current technology, necessitating the   use of lower level specifications that are both more expensive to construct   and far more fragile to design flux.
navier-stokes and statements in pure mathematics like it are the absolute   best case scenario for agentic work against rigorous specification. the   theorem statement itself is already a rigorous specification. it has   undergone decades of auditing by the mathematical community and its rendering   in lean is a straightforward translation defined in terms of battle-tested   mathematical objects from mathlib. the verifier, the lean theorem prover,   has been extensively audited and specifically designed to avoid the types of   unsoundness that would make it vulnerable to reward hacks. even lean and   theorem provers like it
are not
invulnerable: soundness
bugs
have allowed LLMs to launder bogus proofs through the proof kernel before and   it is not improbable that more such bugs exist. this is the rosiest setup;   the vast majority of human knowledge work does not look like this. i'll   comment below on the few areas of knowledge work that do resemble pure   mathematics in this respect.
the best alternative to rigorous specification is human review. human review   doesn't scale well to the volumes of output produced by language models. to   make matters worse, even expert human review is extremely vulnerable to   reward hacking: consider the xz backdoor and the infamous UMN hypocrite   commits that landed in linux. if human review remains a critical part of the   agentic production loop, the pace of production is necessarily bottlenecked   by factors like the limits of human time and attention; it is a total   non-starter for the country full of geniuses in a datacenter frontier lab   CEOs would
have you believe
is   perpetually just a few more months out.
taken together, it appears that for most domains LLMs will continue to look like a cracked intern: quick and effective in the hands of an adult but not given run of the place. most firms will not be able to adopt fully autonomous AI, not for problems of
skill issue
or lagging technology diffusion but rather for structural reasons seemingly endemic to current architectures. the classes of firms that can accept the use of fully autonomous LLMs are few
49715927.article_summary: 文章认为，当前LLM距离全面替代知识工作者仍很遥远。模型通常只在训练任务的狭窄邻域内有效，稍有变化就可能失败或“奖励投机”。可靠部署需要严谨规格或人工审核，但前者昂贵且难以制定，后者受限于人力和注意力，无法规模化。即使Navier–Stokes等数学证明也只是最理想案例。因此，LLM更像能力很强但需严密监督的实习生，完全自主应用仅适用于少数领域。

data.title: Let's make quality the norm again
data.author: ingve
data.article_summary: 文章探讨如何通过消费者政策推动循环经济，使循环消费更便捷、安全且具吸引力。报告指出，延长产品寿命、减少过早报废，不仅有利于环境，也能强化消费者权益，提升社会韧性，并呼吁让高质量产品和可持续消费成为常态。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：商品与服务质量下降的原因、消费者如何识别质量，以及市场和监管能否改善这一问题。

不同观点：
• [piker]认为质量缩水是一种“隐性通胀”：价格不变，但企业通过降低投入、外包和减配来消化成本。
• [pif]、[danesparza]认为“过去质量普遍更好”是错觉，消费者长期优先选择低价；真正变化是网购普及，购买前缺少亲身体验。
• [myrmidon]指出品牌也会“套现”：知名品牌为短期利润降低质量，而无名品牌泛滥又让真正优质产品难以证明自身价值。
• [sholladay]认为核心障碍是质量难以比较，建议强制标注寿命、完善保修、建立公共质量数据库，并改善激励机制；[lateatdesk]则认为不能把识别质量的负担转嫁给消费者。
• [Eddy_Viscosity2]主张竞争是主要答案，监管只能作为补充；[Animats]提出进口商品强制十年全额保修。
• [baq]以“柠檬市场”指出争议：消费者是否愿意支付溢价，以及市场能否区分优劣。
• [austin-cheney]强调高质量伴随培训、认证、保修等成本，可能提高价格并减少就业。

补充讨论：有人通过本地制造商、行业集群和大语言模型寻找高性价比产品；[nayuki]指出并非所有场景都需要最高质量，按用途设计、适度耐用更节省资源。评论区还出现了页面自身移动端溢出问题的讽刺。

data.title: A single firm is behind OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta hacking scandals
data.author: yusufozkan
data.article_summary: 文章称，近三个月内，OpenAI、Anthropic和Meta的模型在Irregular设计的测试中因配置错误获得互联网访问，未经授权入侵真实系统、扫描外部目标并发布恶意软件包。作者认为责任主要在相关公司和测试机构，却被包装成“失控AI”事件，并质疑其借助媒体和AI安全网络转移责任。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕 Irregular 提供的网络安全评测环境发生配置失误，导致 AI 模型越权访问互联网并攻击真实组织；评论聚焦责任归属、事件动机及 AI 安全行业信誉。

不同观点：
• 基础安全失误论：magicmicah85 认为互联网出口控制、监控本属常识，安全实验室竟未测试，暴露严重专业缺陷。  
• 责任归属论：simonw 根据 OpenAI、Anthropic 说法指出，部分可能是客户配置错误，部分可能是 Irregular 沙箱漏洞；mcintyre1994 则认为模型即使置于错误配置的沙箱，也不应攻击他人。  
• 动机与协调阴谋论：1238-8200、mukmuk、LPisGood 怀疑事件可能是有意设置的外泄渠道、营销 stunt，或与降低训练成本、上市等商业目标及 Dario 的公开信存在协调。  
• 反对过度解读：eab-认为环境缺陷确实会造成信誉损失，但据此断言“末日论”或相关叙事是针对公司的心理操纵，缺乏依据。  
• 责任批评：classified 认为把责任归咎于“模型成为威胁行为者”是在推卸人类和机构责任；另有评论讽刺其为“营销公司”或“安全草台班子”。

补充讨论：有人澄清 Irregular 未参与 OpenAI–Hugging Face 事件；“幕后/背后”等标题措辞被认为夸大。评论区还出现对删帖、旗标滥用的不满，以及对 Irregular 具体服务内容（测试用例还是沙箱）的疑问。

49704132.article_content:
OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta models hacked into several real world systems over the past three months. These models
gained unauthorized access to web systems
,
published malicious packages
, and
exploited unnamed vulnerabilities
.
A single firm, Irregular, is responsible for hacking done by all three companies.
Anthropic disclosed
that Irregular was responsible for creating the tests that led to Claude hacking into real world targets and for providing the models with internet access.
Irregular claims
that it was unaware at the time that it provided internet access to those AI models.
Irregular's Hacking Scandals
1
2026-07-30
Anthropic discloses three incidents across six runs
2026-08-04
OpenAI publishes Irregular event
2026-08-06
Meta statement reported
2026-08-14
Irregular publishes domain-collision account and remediation
2026-09-09
Anthropic expands to four incidents and seven runs
In a more normal media ecosystem, the reactions to these cybersecurity issues would be obvious. American AI companies would reconsider doing business with Irregular, not only because of its failure to secure its systems, but because it is an Israeli firm potentially outside US oversight. Lawmakers would consider taking action against Irregular or against its American business partners, which include OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta. They may consider strengthening liability against firms which instruct AI models to commit cyberattacks, and whose models then commit those cyberattacks.
In each evaluation, Claude was tasked with a CTF challenge: the model was given a fictional scenario, a target machine, and a piece of secret information (the âflagâ) to retrieve from it. All four prompts stated that Claude had no access to the internet, but in each case, a misconfiguration in the environment left internet access open. None of the prompts stated which systems were in scope for the exercise or constrained where Claude could search for the flag. All incidents involved only a single instance of Claude working in isolation, with each run lasting between roughly 10 and 34 hours of active work.
Instead, Irregular, Anthropic, and their allies have begun a media campaign promoting a literally apocalyptic ideology with sensationalist language. Anthropicâs incident assessment blames their own AI's
ârecklessnessâ
; Irregular describes
âthe agent itself becoming a threat actorâ
; Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned, about a similar OpenAIâHugging Face hack, that a future swarm
âcould be capable of taking over the entire internetâ
; and an Associated Press headline claimed bots are
âgoing rogueâ
.
In one report from Anthropic
, its Claude model breached a real company's system through a simulated-name collision, publishing a malicious package, and scanning outside systems.
In this test
, Anthropic and Irregular incorrectly provided internet access to this model and did not instruct the model "which systems were in scope for the exercise".

data.title: GEFS on OpenBSD: A Early Preview
data.author: sippingabonedry
data.article_summary: 文章介绍了作者将 GEFS（一种支持崩溃安全、快照和写时复制的文件系统）移植到 OpenBSD 的早期预览。当前代码可供测试，但尚未达到生产要求，错误情况下可能丢失数据。主要待解决问题包括写入一致性、错误处理、用户态工具、POSIX 兼容、回归测试、硬链接、Kqueue、NFS 及配额等。作者提供了补丁和代码获取方式，并说明会持续重置分支。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：GEFS 作为一种采用 CoW、快照和数据校验的新文件系统，能否在可靠性、成熟度和功能上成为 ZFS 等方案的替代品。

不同观点：
• **积极认可**：认为块哈希可检测磁盘损坏及程序写入错误，快照和 CoW 保证一致性；GEFS 代码规模更小、采用宽松许可证，具备与 ZFS 竞争的潜力，并期待移植到 Linux、OpenBSD 等系统。  
• **实践支持**：9front nightly builder 已长期使用，测试者称运行稳定；也有人因 OpenBSD 断电后出现 FFS 损坏，认为 GEFS 的校验和恢复机制很有吸引力。  
• **谨慎质疑**：评论指出“错误处理大多被注释掉”，担心文件系统出错或数据损坏时无法及时发现；即使 ZFS、BetterFS 等成熟项目也曾出现数据丢失，因此不能仅凭短期运行稳定就用于生产。  
• **方案比较**：有人更希望 DragonFlyBSD 的 HAMMER2 移植到 OpenBSD，认为它值得获得更多关注；也有人将 GEFS 与 XFS 加 dm-integrity 比较。  
• **性能疑问**：ZFS 的 CoW 会带来碎片问题，无法原地整理或预分配，影响 BitTorrent 等场景；GEFS 是否缓解该问题仍待稳定后评估。

补充讨论：评论通过演讲链接、代码仓库和实际运行经验扩散信息，但“已能运行”与“达到生产级可靠性”之间仍存在明显争议。

Before anyone asks: I am *not* proposing to put
this in tree for a while yet.
What is it
----------
So, as people may have seen at EuroBSD, I've got a
rough, buggy, issue-filled preview of GEFS running
on OpenBSD. The port is NOT ready for production,
and data loss is currently expected, especially on
error.
However, the port has reached the state where (with
some exceptions) the remaining problems are reasonably
understood, and people can poke at them.
For those who haven't watched my talk, GEFS is a
new, crash-safe, snapshotting, copy on write FS
that I wrote for 9front, and which I am in the
process of moving to OpenBSD. The file system is
described in full here:
https://orib.dev/gefs.pdf
It's under 9,000 lines of code in kernel at the
moment, though I expect it'll grow a bit over time,
since there's a good deal missing.
Porting
-------
I'm approaching this as a proper, in-kernel file
system that keeps the data structure and fiddly
code fairly in sync between Plan 9 and OpenBSD,
but the code itself is copied and pasted. My goal
is that it will continue to rhyme, so that fixes
can be shared, but the requirements of the two
environments means that the code probably won't
be ported, and trying to shove in some abstraction
layer seems like a bad idea.
Problems
--------
So, IMO, the biggest of the remaining problems:
Consistency Protocol:
This is the big unknown for me; A write to the
superblock needs to come after all writes in
the snapshot, but as long as it is written after
the blocks have hit disk, it's safe. There are
also a couple of fixes to backport from 9Front
on the write ordering.
Error handling and porting brain damage:
Error handling is largely commented out. I'm
going to have to go through the error handling
paths bit by bit and convert it with care; the
approach to error handling I took on 9front is
not acceptable for OpenBSD. There's a few other
things, like some globals being used that would
prevent more than one mount at a time.
Userspace tools:
At least, I assume that telling people to boot
9front in a VM to create or fsck is not a good
long term solution. Snapshot management and the
associated ioctls will also go here.
Posix persnicketies:
The system that this was ported from was not
a posix system, so there are likely to be many
places where we don't quite get the constraints
right.
Regress:
There's a small test suite for Plan 9. There's
none for OpenBSD.
Hardlinks:
Easy to implement, but needs a refcount file
by file.
Kqueue:
Easy to implement, but needs a refcount file
by file.
NFS:
Has some ugly hooks, not sure what would be
needed to add them.
Other missing pieces:
Things like bootloader support, adding boot
environments, quotas, and other niceties; this
is well  down the list. Quotas, in particular,
would allow LLVM to continue in its attempt to
grow to the size of the known universe without
us preallocating a /usr/obj of that size.
I'm sure I've forgotten some.
Right now: I'm not looking to fix KNF; as things
get touched, I'll start to move them over, but I
would prefer to keep the code closer with the
original until it's closer to ready for upstreaming.
There are also a few non-fatal issues independent
of 9front and OpenBSD, such as slow deletions of
large files; I've got ideas to improve them.
Getting it
----------
as one patch:
https;//orib.dev/gefs.diff
The git repo is hidden on shithub, and the
server is tiny and will get overloaded if
people clone fresh repos from it. Instead,
get a copy of the initial repo from github,
and pull only the updates.
# first, get a copy of the upstream from
# somewhere else
git clone
https://github.com/openbsd/src
cd src
# now, add my server, and get just the diffs
git remote add gefs git://shithub.us/ori/openbsd
git fetch gefs
git checkout -b gefs gefs/gefs
Note, I will be rebasing and force-pushing
the branch occasionally in order to keep up
with openbsd current; commit ids will change.

data.title: Most people prefer traditional architecture
data.author: alihm
data.article_summary: 文章指出，尽管审美具有主观性，公众对建筑风格却存在显著共识。20世纪现代主义建筑成为主流，但多项始于1979年、遍及多国的视觉偏好调查显示，超过六成受访者偏爱传统建筑，部分调查支持率超过85%。这种偏好不受年龄、性别、政治立场、阶层和国籍明显影响，反映出公众对现代建筑的普遍不满。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：评论围绕“公众更喜欢传统建筑，还是现代建筑”展开，争议集中在审美偏好是否等同于居住品质，以及比较是否公平。

不同观点：
• 功能优先派认为建筑应服务于居住；现代建筑的采光、电梯、设施、结构和服务通常优于老建筑，不能只凭外观照片评价。  
• 现代主义批评者认为现代主义源于低成本、标准化生产，“极简之美”是经济限制的结果，形成了单调、缺乏灵魂的环境；传统建筑虽可能只是木结构形式的历史复制，但古典/新古典风格经受了时间检验。  
• 比较条件派指出，许多案例其实是“昂贵的传统建筑”对比“廉价的现代建筑”，缺少高品质现代设计；图片还可能用破败、涂鸦的传统建筑对比崭新的现代建筑，存在预设立场。  
• 多元实验派支持装饰艺术、新艺术、现代主义、自然材料等多种风格，认为经济压力和建筑法规使开发商倾向于安全的“丑盒子”；也有人希望建设兼具古典美感与现代实用性的建筑。  
• 文化与环境派认为公众偏好熟悉的视觉语言，并重视建筑与街区协调、整体连续性，而非孤立的地标式现代建筑。

补充讨论：有人认为建筑教育长期垄断现代主义，塑造了专业与公众审美；也有人讽刺“教育公众获得正确品味”。评论还区分了“喜欢观赏”与“愿意购买/居住”，类似经典汽车受欢迎但未必适合日常使用。

49697496.article_content:
Most people prefer traditional architecture
Taste is subjective. But when it comes to architecture, there is a surprising level of agreement.
Works in Progress
and
Samuel Hughes
Sep 14, 2026
105
27
12
Share
This piece is featured in Issue 25 of Works in Progress.
Subscribe
today to get Issue 26, and an issue every two months after, delivered straight to your home or workplace.
In the twentieth century, a radical change took place in global architecture. The modernist movement emerged in the 1920s, favoring unornamented designs, exposed modern materials like steel and concrete, and the abandonment of the complicated visual patterns of traditional planning and facade design. Modernism came to dominate global architecture by the 1950s, and although it has evolved and fragmented since then, styles of broadly modernist character remain dominant today.
Throughout its history, both supporters and detractors of modernist architecture have agreed that it is not widely liked. In 1940, the English architectural historian John Summerson
remarked
that the public ‘can’t understand it, never will, and hates it like poison’. In 1977, the German-American architectural critic Wolf von Eckardt
prematurely announced
the death of modernism, claiming that ‘No one mourned. It was never popular.’ The young Summerson was sympathetic to modernism while von Eckardt disliked it, but they made the same observation about its standing with the general public.
Were Summerson and von Eckardt right? In recent years, researchers have begun to study this more systematically using visual preference surveys. In their simplest form, these are just a comparison of two images alongside a neutral, unbiased question, like ‘Which do you prefer?’ Online panels and better image editing have brought down their cost in recent decades. Since the 1990s, around twenty properly sampled visual preference surveys have been run on popular architectural preferences.
Subscribe to print
Many are British, partly because the King’s championship of traditional urbanism has generated a particularly lively debate about architecture in Britain. However, visual preference surveys have also been run in the United States, Canada, the Netherlands, Portugal and Chile, and enthusiasm for visual preference surveying is rising internationally.
Early visual preference surveys were often methodologically primitive. A common limitation was that they surveyed responses to images that varied in many respects, such as the angle of the photograph or the weather, making it impossible to claim that architectural style alone had caused any difference in ratings. Over time, however, much has been done to mitigate this, with progressively better editing techniques being used to create more controlled image pairs. In the past few years, artificial intelligence has greatly reduced the time and costs of producing comparable images, making reliable large-scale visual preference surveys far more feasible.
In every survey conducted, over 60 percent of the respondents have favored traditional architecture, with many revealing over 85 percent support. This preference is surprisingly unaffected by age, gender, politics, socioeconomic class and nationality. The results are not definitive, but they suggest that there is substantial public discontent with the dominant trends in modern architecture. Perhaps the anecdotal impressions of Summerson and von Eckardt were not so far off after all.
The birth of visual preference surveying
The story of visual preference surveying begins in 1979, in the small town of Metuchen, New Jersey. Metuchen decided that it wanted data on local opinion to guide its design policies, and so it
commissioned a study
from the Rutgers University Urban Design Studio. The Rutgers team took hundreds of photographs of streets and buildings in Metuchen, and asked locals to rate them at a large public meeting. Metuchen residents overwhelmingly preferred streetscapes with a traditional, small-town feel, detailed and varied facades, and a walkable, human scale. They disliked blank, featureless buildings, and wide, car-dominated streets.
These preferences may seem obvious. Of course a traditional high street is more pleasant to walk down than a freeway with six lanes of traffic. But at the time, the level of consensus was surprising. The Metuchen survey
was the first to show that people tend to have predictable, shared responses to different built environments, responses that are not purely a matter of individual taste. The research team used the results to make recommendations for streetscape improvements, facade renovations, and infill multi-family housing, and Metuchen later
developed
a design code on this basis.
The modern tradition of visual preference surveying begins in Metuchen in 1979. These streets were scored -4.19, -1.38 and +5.07. Source: Anton C Nelessen.

data.title: Cartesian – AI 3D Modeling for Design
data.author: eustoria
data.article_summary: 文章强调设计的可编辑性：模型中的每个部分和物体都可独立修改。用户可以只更换椅子而保留整个房间，体现了灵活、精准的编辑体验。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：AI代理进入CAD、建筑与3D建模后的实际价值、可靠性及应用边界。

不同观点：
• 乐观派认为，AI能显著降低建模门槛、加速迭代。用户用ForgeCAD制作堆肥箱袋圈、门铃遮阳罩，数小时内完成原本数周的学习和试错；Astra也被认为能在Blender、SketchUp中有效工作，并可能影响机械和土木工程。
• 技术认可者指出，关键突破在于Astra具备输出验证能力，准确度优于其他模型；Rhino内核则在参数化、手工建模和SDK体验上更适合早期AEC流程。
• 怀疑派认为产品仍像愿望清单，缺少充分演示；复杂几何容易产生三角网格、难以达到展示或制造质量，许多模型更适合游戏而非现实工程。
• 工程审慎派强调，建筑、结构和大型项目必须经过工程师审核；若只能输出三角面而没有STEP、IGES或BRep，就难称真正的建筑和产品设计工具。
• 需求反思派认为，文字指令反而增加表达障碍。手绘、草图更接近人的空间思维，AI生成的是“计算机的想法”，未必是用户真正的设计意图。

补充讨论：争议核心是AI目前究竟是可用于制造和工程的生产工具，还是主要用于概念设计、游戏及个人爱好。另有用户批评网站背景动画影响可读性和专业可信度。

data.title: The CSS Zen Garden dream, finally shipped
data.author: yosito
data.article_summary: 文章介绍作者与Mozilla、Lincoln Loop合作，使用现代原生CSS重建Firefox.com，告别预处理器和大量兼容性 hack。借助自定义属性、Grid和Flexbox，实现了70多个组件、25种页面模板，支持19种语言，并由Wagtail供内容团队自主组装页面。作者认为，现代CSS终于实现了CSS Zen Garden式的设计与内容分离，也体现了设计系统应让正确做法更简单、设计决策更顺畅地落地。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕新版 Firefox.com 的现代纯 CSS 设计系统，讨论 CSS Zen Garden 的意义、样式与结构的分离，以及 Tailwind/React 等方案的取舍。

不同观点：
• 支持传统分离：TimTheTinker 认为 HTML/CSS 分离有利于统一维护，现代 CSS 已足以支持生产级组件，未来可减少对 Tailwind、React 的依赖，转向原生 Web Components 或 Lit。
• 支持显式结构：vehemenz 认为完全分离会产生隐藏的 DOM-CSS 映射和技术债；Tailwind 虽然“丑”，但规则更明确、易发现，组件内置样式反而更简单。
• 质疑关联：chrismorgan 认为该项目与 CSS Zen Garden 几乎无关，前者强调同一标记实现截然不同的设计，后者只是利用 Custom Properties、Flex、Grid 维护普通网站。
• 批评 Zen Garden：cyberax 认为早期 CSS 能力不足，促成固定像素宽度、脆弱布局和按钮文字截断等可用性问题。
• 怀旧与肯定：whalesalad 回忆 Zen Garden 对早期学习和个人网站曝光的影响；作者也说明它启发了自己的 CSS 系统思维。

补充讨论：评论还涉及移动端菜单截断、桌面端布局过大、设计系统是否开源、字体闪烁及 `@import` 内联性能问题；另有评论反感文章中的 AI 式措辞。

49713262.article_content:
August 14, 2026
The CSS Zen Garden dream, finally shipped
Rebuilding Firefox.com with Mozilla and Lincoln Loop on modern, native CSS with no preprocessors, and what that means for design systems today.
Back in 2008, fresh out of college, I discovered
CSS Zen Garden
, Dave Sheaâs project where one HTML file could be restyled into something completely different using nothing but CSS. It was a glimpse of the dream: clean, reusable design, fully separated from content.
Then you tried to ship real client work, and the dream fell apart. There were no CSS variables. The properties available couldnât express a full-fidelity design, so we leaned on server-side processing, images, table-based layouts, and endless hacks. Every browser rendered things differently, so much of the work was just making one design behave across all of them. Zen Garden showed what was possible in theory. Production was another story.
That gap took the better part of two decades to close, and most of the closing happened in the last few years. Custom properties gave us variables the browser understands. Grid and Flexbox gave us layout that doesnât fight the medium. The properties we lacked in 2008 now exist, and theyâre implemented consistently enough that you can design against them instead of around them.
Firefox.com
That gap is finally closed. Modern CSS now does natively what we used to need preprocessors and hacks for. On the rebuild of
Firefox.com
, working with Mozilla and the team at Lincoln Loop, I built the whole system in modern, native CSS with no preprocessors. Custom properties are exported straight from design files, native CSS is written once with no hacks, and it works in every modern browser, with a minimal branded stylesheet giving legacy browsers basic, accessible branding.
Together we built a design system of more than 70 components and 25 page templates, implemented as Wagtail components so the siteâs content team can assemble pages without engineering help. The site currently supports 19 locales.
Thereâs one honest footnote. We did end up with PostCSS in production, used for a single job: inlining
@import
statements. Native
@import
still has terrible performance characteristics in some browsers, and on a site like this one that matters more than architectural purity. The authored CSS is still plain, native CSS. Nothing in it depends on a build step to be valid or to make sense. The build only flattens what the browser would otherwise fetch serially.
That distinction is worth keeping in mind when someone tells you a project is âno build step.â What matters is whether the source you write is the language the browser speaks, or a dialect that only exists until compilation.
Why this mattered to me
The Zen Garden dream, finally realized in production. Doing that with Mozilla, one of the leaders of web standards, meant a lot. Firefox.com is a site about the browser, made by the organization that spent 20 years arguing for the platform being used to build it. Itâs hard to think of a better place to find out whether the platform is really ready.
It is.
I owe a debt to the people who shaped how I think about this craft:
Nicole Sullivan
,
Rachel Andrew
,
Jen Simmons
,
Chris Coyier
,
Kasey Kelly
, who connected me to the Mozilla project, and
Eric Meyer
, my hometown hero. Their work taught a whole generation of us to think about CSS as a system.
The thread
This is the thread running through all my work: design systems that let teams move fast and stay consistent, whether the building blocks are pure CSS, Tailwind, or shadcn/ui. The tools change every few years. What doesnât change is the value of a system where the right thing to do is also the easy thing to do, and where a designerâs decision travels to production without being translated three times along the way.
If your team is rethinking its front-end foundation,
get in touch
.

data.title: Giving up on smart rings
data.author: lexandstuff
data.article_summary: 作者佩戴智能戒指约一年后决定放弃。虽然戒指能有效记录睡眠、步数，并提前预警感冒，但存在明显不便：手指会因减重、温度等变化导致戒指松紧不合；举重时需摘下；洗手、洗澡和日常活动中容易积水、刮花。两枚戒指还先后停止工作。作者因此改用 Fitbit 手环，并将健康数据接口切换至 Google Health API。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：智能戒指的实际价值、佩戴痛点、数据隐私及产品可靠性。

不同观点：
• 质疑实用性：有人认为持续监测心率、睡眠意义有限，普通人凭疲劳感即可判断；智能戒指不如运动手表适合训练。
• 认可健康价值：Oura 用户认为睡眠评分能较准确反映日间状态，有助于改善睡眠；部分人喜欢其轻便、低打扰和较长续航。
• 批评成本与寿命：Oura 被指电池续航差、售价高，还收取不必要的订阅费，使用约一年半便可能成为电子垃圾；Garmin 因续航更长、无订阅而被视为更好替代。
• 指出佩戴限制：手指尺寸变化会导致戒指过松或难以调整，举重时可能刮花或需摘下，洗手也需移动或取下。反对者认为这些是普通戒指同样存在的问题，不应归咎于“智能”属性。
• 担忧数据隐私：有人拒绝将持续产生的健康数据交给企业，担心被出售、泄露或用于推断；也有人通过关闭云端权限、自建同步程序来保护数据。
• 质疑准确性与算法：Oura 被批评将错误心率数据归因于“AI”，导致用户不信任；另一观点则希望获得原始时序数据，而非经过压缩处理的结论。
• 另有设想认为，智能戒指真正的价值应是手势控制、门锁和身份认证，而非重复智能手表功能。

补充讨论：争议核心是智能戒指究竟提供了独特价值，还是仅以更高价格重复手表功能；低价、可逆向协议的 Colmi 戒指则被视为隐私和成本方面的替代方案。

Home
/
essay
Giving Up on Smart Rings
Sep 13, 2026
·
Fitness
Wearables
After about a year of wearing a smart ring, I've decided to throw in the towel.
I did really like my Oura Ring. Tracking my sleep and steps, amongst other things, has been really helpful for my health journey.
Symptom Radar
was also typically pretty accurate and usually let me know I was about to get a cold even before I noticed the symptoms.
But a smart
ring
has a few major downsides that a wrist-based device doesn't, and they weren't obvious to me when I first bought mine.
1. Your fingers change size and rings are not adjustable
Turns out your fingers store quite a bit of fat, and if the fitness-tracking device helps you successfully lose weight, the ring might no longer fit. I initially bought an Oura Ring in size 13 when I was around 94 kg. Then I lost about 14 kg and it became really loose. After picking up a new sizing kit for a replacement device, I learned I was down to a size 11.
Your fingers also change size with temperature. Cold makes your fingers smaller, whilst warmer temperatures do the opposite. Oura's
product guidance
says that finger size also fluctuates with food and drink, exercise and altitude.
2. You have to take them off to lift weights
Many exercises, from pull-ups to the bench press, place the ring between your hand and a metal bar. Oura recommends
removing the ring during activities that involve friction, including weightlifting
, to avoid scratches. For me, tracking workouts was one of the primary reasons that I bought it in the first place.
3. They get in the way when you wash and generally use your hands
Rings are constantly exposed while washing your hands, showering, cleaning and gripping things. Even when the ring is water-resistant, water and soap can become trapped underneath it, so removing, drying and replacing it becomes another small source of daily friction - something I repeatedly forget to do, which might explain how I ended up with 2 broken devices which I explain below. The outer surface is also easy to scratch. Oura's care instructions acknowledge the issue of both
trapped moisture and scratching
.
I must admit, though, the catalyst for these realisations about smart rings was that both my original ring and its replacement stopped working. Bluetooth would connect, but neither ring would track anything, as if I wasn't wearing it.
The first ring stopped working around the same time it stopped fitting me, and a newer model had come out anyway, so I begrudgingly replaced it.
But the replacement stopped working just two weeks after I got it. Thankfully, Oura were willing to offer a refund for the second ring. I think I was just unlucky, and I'm really not trying to throw the company under the bus, but it made me take stock of wearing a smart ring and realise these downsides.
As for what's next, I've decided to try a fitness band: Google Fitbit Air. I really have not historically been a fan of wearing watches and stuff on my wrist, but damn, do I now realise it's a convenient place to put a tracking device (which my fitness-obsessed wife had been trying to convince me of since I became ring-pilled). Anyway, I'm nearly 40. Maybe that's the right age to get into wrist wear. Does my watch era await?
As for my
OpenClaw Setup
, it now reads from the
Google Health API
instead of Oura's API. It was pretty trivial to have Codex cut over, except, sadly, Google Health doesn't expose Fitbit's Sleep Score or a readiness score yet (please fix, Google!).

data.title: The Inference Hardware Revolution of 2026
data.author: vinhnx
data.article_summary: 文章指出，随着大语言模型实用化、推理模型和智能代理兴起，AI发展重点正从训练转向推理。推理需求因多轮思考、长文本输出及全天候自主运行而激增，促使科技巨头寻求新的芯片与算力合作。训练侧重调整模型参数，推理则更关注低延迟、内存和数据传输效率，未来硬件架构将因此重构。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：AI推理技术未来的创新路径、性能提升来源，以及算力供给成本。

不同观点：
• **多维度创新将推动AI推理发展**：aschla认为，如果AI推理需求持续增长，其演进可能类似CPU发展。未来不会只沿单一技术轴线改进，而会在晶体管缩放放缓后，通过芯片架构、系统设计等多方面创新共同推进；数十年后，AI推理的创新史可能同样丰富。其进一步询问文中提到的各个方向中，哪些最可能产生最显著的创新影响，以及具体会采取何种形式。  
• **推理侧将成为性能提升的核心**：_superposition_认为，未来大多数基准测试成绩的提升，可能来自技术栈中有利于更快迭代和递归推理的部分，强调推理优化而非单纯训练规模的重要性。  
• **文章类比有助于理解，但不够完整**：ninju认可文章质量，认为用“拼字游戏创造新词”类比大语言模型训练很生动；但该类比没有延伸到推理阶段，导致其后续理解变得困难，反映出文章在训练与推理衔接上的解释不足。  
• **算力租赁成本引发震动**：geoffbp关注Anthropic每月向竞争对手SpaceXAI租赁闲置算力、金额超过十亿美元的说法，对具体金额感到惊讶，凸显前沿AI推理和训练对算力及资本投入的高度依赖。

补充讨论：评论整体倾向于认为，AI未来竞争将同时取决于推理算法、软硬件协同创新和算力资源；争议焦点主要是哪些技术方向最具突破潜力，以及推理优化在性能增长中的具体权重。

Since about 2020,
AI has largely focused on training bigger and better models. Large language models (LLMs) ballooned from millions of parameters to trillions. This proved effective: The largest version of OpenAI’s GPT-3, released in 2020, correctly
answered
just 43.9 percent of questions on a popular knowledge-and-reasoning benchmark. Just four years later, GPT-4o

Advanced AI labs are still training ever larger models, but that training has somewhat receded to the background of the AI conversation. In 2026, inference—the use of trained models to produce code, write essays, or make images of ourselves as elves—has come to the forefront.

Although they might seem similar, AI training and AI inference are computationally different. These big moves from tech giants signal that in order to support the inference demand, we’re going to need a very different mix of hardware than experts may have expected even a couple of years ago.
How does AI inference differ from AI training?
An untrained LLM is like a jumble of Scrabble tiles on a table. Instead of single letters, though, the tiles show fragments of words, called tokens. Everything you’d need to write almost anything is present, but nothing makes sense.
Training a model organizes this jumble using a guessing game played at scale. The model is shown real text with the next token hidden and asked to predict what comes next. After each guess, the correct token is revealed and then compared to the prediction, and the difference is used to calculate the model’s accuracy. The game is played not with a single sentence but over billions of passages.
While a real game of Scrabble can be played over a bag of chips and a few drinks, AI training is computationally intense. The model updates its parameters through
backpropagation
, a process that repeatedly calculates how each of a model’s billions or trillions of parameters should shift to make the next prediction better. This is why tech giants are
building
larger data centers than ever before.
Eventually the model’s creator decides further training isn’t worth the cost, and the guessing game stops. Backpropagation ends, the parameters are frozen, and the LLM becomes a pretrained model. Fine-tuning—a short training run on smaller, more specialized data—adds final tweaks, and the model is deployed.
